source_text: Ille dixit: Gratia ex multis delictis in iustificationem [n175] ; ille peccati efficientiae medicinae copiam praetulit; qui sensus catholicorum dogmati congruit intellegentium in his remissionem peccatorum fieri, in quibus possunt multa deprehendi, id est motu propriae voluntatis attracta, in quibus autem non sit hic motus propriae voluntatis, id est in parvulis, non minus nulla esse quam multa.
pass_a_gloss: He said: Grace from many offenses into justification; he preferred the plenty of medicine to the efficiency of sin; which sense agrees with the dogma of catholics understanding that a remission of sins is made in those in whom many can be caught, that is drawn by a motion of proper will, but in those in whom this motion of proper will is not, that is in little children, there are no less none than many.

lemmas.lexica: LS delictum; Blaise Rom 5 delictum vs donum
LS iustificatio; Blaise forensic making-just, not later system
LS peccatum=fault, error; Blaise Christian sin
LS voluntas=will, wish; Blaise moral will
LS gratia=favor; Blaise grace; in iustitia definitions often 'favoritism'

pass_b_english: He said, ‘Grace is from many offenses to justification’ (Romans 5:16). He ranked the abundance of the medicine above sin’s effectiveness. This meaning agrees with the catholics’ doctrine. They understand that remission of sins takes place in those in whom many sins can be found—sins acquired by the movement of their own will. But where this movement of a personal will does not exist, that is, in infants, there are no sins at all, not merely no multitude of sins.

choices.why: Paul's delictum of the one man; an act, not a nature.
Paul's iustificatio vitae; keep forensic making-just, not a later systematic slogan as default.

speaker: Julian of Eclanum (words preserved in Augustine, Opus imperfectum contra Iulianum); Augustine's reply at this locus is excluded.
